headline: Databricks hits $188B valuation, extending its run as AI’s favorite second act
summary: The data and AI company announced a new funding round led by Coatue, pushing its valuation to an astonishing $188 billion, a significant jump from $134 billion just five months ago.
details: Databricks announced a new funding round, led by Coatue, valuing the company at $188 billion. While the exact amount raised wasn't disclosed, reports suggest it's around $3 billion, with the round set to close later this summer.
It's unusual to announce funding before it's in hand, but a VC source indicated the deal is solid due to high investor demand. This marks another rapid increase in valuation for the company.
This latest raise continues Databricks' aggressive fundraising streak over the past 18 months, as it successfully repositioned itself from a big data SaaS provider to a leading AI company.

Just five months prior, in February, Databricks secured a $5 billion Series L raise at a $134 billion valuation. This followed a $1 billion raise at $100 billion in September 2025, and a record-breaking $10 billion at $62 billion in December 2024.
The company, founded in 2013, initially thrived in the big data era by providing software for storing and analyzing vast amounts of enterprise data in the cloud.

Leveraging its existing troves of enterprise data, Databricks was perfectly positioned to meet the growing demand for AI solutions that offered the same security and governance as traditional enterprise software.
Databricks has rapidly rolled out a suite of AI products, including Lakebase, a database for AI agents, Unity, an AI gateway, and Omnigent, a 'meta-harness' for managing multiple agents.
The company has also championed the adoption of more affordable open-weight models, particularly Z.ai’s GLM 5.2 for coding, as a key strategy for cost control in 2026.

Internal benchmarking by Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi showed that open models, especially GLM 5.2, can handle high-difficulty coding tasks at a lower total cost than proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

Crucially, the study also found that the choice of 'harness'—the agentic coding tool wrapping the model—equally impacted costs. Open-source harnesses like Pi proved highly effective in managing context and reducing expenses without sacrificing quality.
This strategic shift and successful integration of AI offerings have solidified Databricks' image as a formidable AI company, fueling its impressive valuation growth.

headline_marked: [[VC uses Zoom name to block AI transcription]] as always-on recording becomes ubiquitous
headline: VC uses Zoom name to block AI transcription as always-on recording becomes ubiquitous
summary: A new trend of AI transcription apps leads a VC to change his Zoom name to explicitly deny consent, highlighting growing privacy concerns. Many now assume meetings are recorded.
details: VC Jeremy Levine now uses his Zoom name to explicitly state "I do not consent to transcribing or recording," a direct response to the rise of AI transcription apps. This tactic highlights a growing concern over privacy in digital meetings.

The ubiquity of always-on recording, driven by new AI note-taking apps and devices, is changing social norms. Many professionals, like VC Eric Bahn, now automatically assume meetings are being recorded.
The trend extends beyond professional settings; one founder reportedly uses the Granola app to record first dates. She then feeds the transcript to Claude to analyze her engagement and empathy.

Levine calls this widespread recording "socially unacceptable behavior" that stifles spontaneous conversation. Others point out the potential legal complexities and the risk of creating an "audio landfill" of unreviewed content.
